abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a foundational theory of situated program repair that fundamentally reconceptualizes how automated debugging systems interact with code context. Traditional repair approaches treat bugs as isolated defects, but we propose that repair effectiveness emerges from the dynamic interplay between the program's semantic structure, developer intent signals, and environmental constraints. We introduce the Context-Situated Repair Formalism (CSRF), a mathematical framework that models these three dimensions as coupled constraints in a修复 search space. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that CSRF captures repair scenarios unreachable by existing semantics-based or learning-based methods, revealing fundamental limitations in current automated debugging paradigms. We prove that optimal repair under CSRF is decidable for first-order theories and establish complexity bounds for practical fragments. The framework enables a new class of repair algorithms that reason about contextual appropriateness rather than mere syntactic correctness. This work opens theoretical horizons for automated software engineering by shifting the locus of repair from individual statements to program-context-environment triplets, establishing foundations for future systems that understand why code fails within its operational context rather than merely what fails.

We present a significantly strengthened theoretical analysis of counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) that addresses its fundamental scalability limitations in program synthesis tasks. Prior theoretical work established that CEGIS achieves polynomial-time synthesis in languages where verification is polynomial-time, but this guarantee relies on idealized assumptions about the quality of counterexamples and the finiteness of candidate spaces. We develop a refined analysis that accounts for realistic scenarios with noisy specifications and infinite candidate domains. Our main contribution is the Bounded-Confidence CEGIS framework, which provides tighter complexity bounds by exploiting monotonicity properties in specification satisfaction. We prove that our approach reduces the sample complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n) for monotone specifications while preserving completeness guarantees. Furthermore, we introduce a novel characterization of the synthesis bottleneck in terms of specification entropy, revealing when CEGIS will and will not scale in practice. These theoretical results explain empirical observations from existing synthesis systems and provide principled guidance for designing more efficient program synthesis algorithms. Our analysis also yields practical recommendations for when to apply counterexample-guided versus traditional enumerative synthesis approaches.

We introduce Synaptic, a novel automated software engineering environment that fundamentally reimagines the integration of large language models with formal verification tools. Unlike existing approaches that treat AI assistance and formal methods as orthogonal concerns, Synaptic implements a tightly-coupled architecture where language model generation and formal specification mining operate bidirectionally. The system continuously refines both the code under development and its formal specifications through a closed-loop process: formal verification queries guide the LLM toward specification-compliant code, while LLM-generated code patterns inform the mining of more precise specifications. Synaptic introduces specification automata, a new representation that captures requirements as both natural language embeddings and formal logic simultaneously, enabling seamless translation between informal intent and verifiable properties. Our implementation includes novel mechanisms for handling specification ambiguity through user-in-the-loop clarification and for maintaining formal guarantees even as code evolves through AI-assisted modifications. We evaluated Synaptic on 847 real-world software engineering tasks spanning embedded systems, web applications, and security-critical code. The system demonstrated the ability to produce formally verified implementations from natural language requirements with 73% success rate, compared to 31% for state-of-the-art pipeline approaches, while maintaining stronger correctness guarantees than any prior AI-assisted development environment.

We present TestForge, a significantly enhanced automated testing system that advances the state of the art in search-based software engineering through novel fitness landscape modeling and adaptive search strategies. While existing genetic improvement approaches treat test generation as static optimization over fixed fitness landscapes, TestForge dynamically characterizes and responds to landscape structure by maintaining per-branch coverage models and detecting deceptive regions where improving one coverage dimension degrades others. The system introduces cascade mutation operators that intelligently adjust mutation rates based on real-time fitness landscape analysis, directing search effort toward promising regions identified through gradient approximation. We implemented TestForge as an extension to the EvoSuite framework, adding 47,000 lines of code that handle landscape-aware evolution, and evaluated it against 12 state-of-the-art automated testing tools across 156 open-source Java projects. TestForge achieved 34% higher branch coverage on average, generated tests that exposed 23 previously unknown bugs (compared to 9 for the best baseline), and reduced redundant test generation by 41%. Particularly notable improvements occurred in challenging scenarios with complex control flow and highly interdependent branches where existing tools struggled. The system's adaptive capabilities also demonstrated 58% faster convergence to high-coverage solutions, making it practical for integration into continuous integration pipelines.
